description: Eight pillars, five anchored questions each. Bump the version whenever a question or anchor changes; saved answers are keyed to it.

pillars.name: Digital public infrastructure
pillars.tests: Open, interoperable rails at population scale

items.q: Is there a universal digital ID with open authentication APIs that the private sector can use?
items.a1: No digital ID, or paper only
items.a3: Digital ID covers most people; private use is limited or costly
items.a5: Near-universal ID; open, low-cost authentication used across sectors

items.q: Is there a real-time, interoperable payment rail with low or zero transaction cost?
items.a1: Payments are cash or closed-loop wallets
items.a3: Real-time rail exists; interoperability or cost limits use
items.a5: Interoperable, near-zero-cost rail used daily by most adults and merchants

items.q: Are DPI components built on open standards and open APIs, without vendor lock-in?
items.a3: Some open APIs; key components still locked in
items.a5: Open specifications; multiple providers compete on the same rails

items.q: Do digital credentials reach the last mile, including rural and low-literacy users?
items.a3: Digital credentials exist, mostly used in cities
items.a5: Verifiable credentials used widely, with assisted and offline access

items.q: Can existing DPI be used as a channel to deliver AI services?
items.a3: Rails exist, but AI pilots are built separately
items.a5: AI services delivered over existing rails at scale

pillars.name: Trusted data ecosystems
pillars.tests: Whether data can flow, and train models, under control

items.q: Is a consent-based data-sharing architecture (DEPA or Account Aggregator type) live?
items.a3: Live in one sector, or in pilots
items.a5: Live at scale in several sectors

items.q: Are high-value public datasets discoverable, curated and available for AI?
items.a3: A national portal exists; quality and coverage are uneven
items.a5: Curated, documented datasets across priority sectors, widely used

items.q: Can models be trained on sensitive data without the data leaving its custodian?
items.a3: Clean rooms, federated learning or other PETs in pilots
items.a5: Privacy-preserving training is routine and has a legal basis

items.q: Are there clear rules for using non-personal and anonymised data?
items.a5: Clear rules in force and applied

items.q: Are there data-quality, metadata and provenance standards for training data?
items.a5: National standards used across data providers

pillars.name: Identity and consent
pillars.tests: Whether consent is granular, revocable, auditable and works for AI

items.q: Is strong authentication (OTP, biometric, face) available to everyone?
items.a3: Available to some groups or channels
items.a5: Available to nearly all, with assisted options

items.q: Is consent granular, revocable, auditable and machine-readable?
items.a1: Blanket consent on paper or click-through
items.a5: A standard consent artefact used across sectors

items.q: Do licensed consent managers operate across sectors?
items.a3: Defined in law; not yet operating at scale
items.a5: Several licensed managers operating across sectors

items.q: Does consent cover AI-specific purposes, such as training versus inference, and AI agents acting for a person?
items.a3: Discussed in policy; no working mechanism
items.a5: Purpose-specific AI consent and agent delegation in use

items.q: Are grievance and redress mechanisms in place, and do people use them?
items.a3: Exist, but slow or little used
items.a5: Fast, digital, widely used, with published outcomes

pillars.name: Compute and models
pillars.tests: Affordable compute and sovereign or open models

items.q: Can startups, academia and the public sector get affordable shared GPU compute?
items.a3: Subsidised access exists; supply is short of demand
items.a5: Ample, affordable access with fair allocation

items.q: Is there a sovereign or trusted cloud for sensitive workloads?
items.a3: Some government cloud; limited AI capacity
items.a5: Trusted cloud with AI capacity for government and regulated sectors

items.q: Is there a funded roadmap for chips, data centres and energy that matches AI demand?
items.a3: Plans exist; delivery or energy lags
items.a5: Funded roadmap on track with demand

items.q: Are there national or open foundation models, including for local languages?
items.a5: Competitive models widely used in public and private services

items.q: Is compute allocated transparently to priority use-cases?
items.a3: Allocation exists, with little published data
items.a5: Transparent, criteria-based allocation with published results

pillars.name: Talent and capability
pillars.tests: Skills across citizens, engineers, researchers and officials

items.q: Is AI and data literacy part of school, university and vocational curricula?
items.a5: Built into core curricula nationwide

items.q: Is there a large enough pipeline of AI engineers, and is talent retained?
items.a5: Large pool; net inflow of experienced talent

items.q: Can government officials procure, evaluate and govern AI?
items.a3: Capacity in a few central units
items.a5: Trained teams across ministries and states

items.q: Are there reskilling programmes for workers affected by AI?
items.a5: Large-scale programmes with tracked outcomes

items.q: Is there frontier AI research capacity (labs, PhDs, publications, academic compute)?
items.a5: Globally competitive research at scale

pillars.name: Regulatory readiness
pillars.tests: Governance that is clear, proportionate and sector-aware

items.q: Is there an AI governance framework with a named institutional owner?
items.a5: Clear framework, owner and review cycle

items.q: Are sector regulators (finance, health, telecom) issuing AI guidance?
items.a5: Most high-risk sectors covered and consistent

items.q: Are there institutions for AI safety testing and evaluation?
items.a3: Institute set up; limited testing capacity
items.a5: Regular testing, benchmarks and red-teaming in use

items.q: Are there legal tools for deepfakes, liability and copyright in training data?
items.a5: Clear, enforced rules on all three

items.q: Are sandboxes or techno-legal designs used, so compliance is built into systems?
items.a5: Techno-legal design standard across AI rails

pillars.name: Public-private collaboration
pillars.tests: Neutral institutions and room for others to build on public rails

items.q: Are there neutral, non-profit institutions running shared rails (NPCI or Sahamati type)?
items.a5: Several, with clear governance

items.q: Do open-source and volunteer communities contribute to DPI and AI design?
items.a5: A recognised, sustained part of design

items.q: Can startups and small firms win public AI projects?
items.a5: Routine, with simple procurement routes

items.q: Is there blended public, private and philanthropic funding for AI public goods?
items.a5: Sustained, pooled funding

items.q: Can private innovators build on public rails without needing permission?
items.a5: Open access under published rules

pillars.name: Inclusion, trust and impact
pillars.tests: Reach, language, measured outcomes and public trust

items.q: Are AI services available in the main local languages, and by voice?
items.a5: Most languages, voice-first, in public services

items.q: Are there measured outcome metrics for AI deployments?
items.a5: Published metrics for major deployments

items.q: Is public trust in data and AI use measured and reported?
items.a5: Regular surveys and transparency reports

items.q: Are bias, fairness and accessibility audits required for public-facing AI?
items.a5: Required, with published results

items.q: Does the country share its DPI and AI building blocks with other countries?
items.a5: A systematic programme with adopters
